newsitem.title: FRANCE: Old deals trigger aggressive EU wheat refund bids.
newsitem.headline: Old deals trigger aggressive EU wheat refund bids.

text.p: An aggressive start to bidding for European Union grain export subsidies has been partly driven by the need to close old contracts, grain traders said on Thursday.
Despite world prices $20 per tonne below French wheat some traders bid for refunds hardly above zero, in the first regular auction of the 1997/98 (July/June) export campaign.
The lowest bid of 0.47 Ecus per tonne for 25,000 tonnes was equivalent to some $145 per tonne compared with U.S. soft red winter pegged at $127 per tonne for September.
The highest bid was 15.87 Ecus, making a wider than usual spread between the highest and lowest submissions.
Traders said left-over business included old contracts to deliver wheat to Cuba and Iraq. Volumes were unavailable.
Last season's wheat sales to Iraq under an oil-for-food plan were partly held up by delays in getting United Nations approval for each contract.
Traders said earlier they expected the European Commission to accept bids for refunds up to five Ecus per tonne, though the most cautious estimates were for three Ecus per tonne.
Granting a maximum refund of three Ecus would allow out a volume of 170,000 tonnes. Granting five Ecus would give a volume of 238,000 tonnes, based on bids received through France.
The tender is the first chance to secure wheat in any quantity since the EU virtually halted wheat exports in April.
It feared then that drought was damaging the new crop and that internal prices would bolt higher on further exports.
But improved conditions now point to a big harvest and EU officials have said they are keen to export before the going becomes too rough. U.S. crops also look better than expected.
The surging dollar helps to keep down refunds at a time when farm budgets are becoming tight.
"Brussels has no reason to refuse everything," said one exporter, adding that a two-week gap before the next tender was another reason not to hold everything back.

European officials have started to express concern over the large new crop, especially of feed grain, saying it could blow a hole in the EU's cautious export subsidy budget and raise the chances of tension over subsidies with Washington.
This season's export subsidy budget was drawn up when world prices were closer to $150 a tonne and is believed be based on similar levels on average throughout the campaign.
EU member-country grain experts met in Brussels earlier on Thursday to discuss the harvest.
No figures were circulated in advance of the meeting but the European Commission said last week it expected a crop of 200 million tonnes against a record 201.5 million last year.
